_comment: Art asset registry. Single source of truth for the generation pipeline. See ../guidelines/art-pipeline.md. Every asset is declared here BEFORE it is drawn; status walks slot -> inbox -> art.

world-prop.note: Top-down orthographic. Drawn in the world at `world` px (camera is 1:1). Baked at 4x display like boat parts.

terrain.note: Reserved. Islands/shore are procedural today (bakeIslandSprite); this profile exists so the rework has a home.

texture.note: Seamless tiling ground fill — repeated across a land polygon, not placed like a sprite. The camera is 1:1, so the square draws at `tileWorld` px on screen and the 1024 master is a 2x supersample. Opaque and full-bleed, so it takes ingest's static path and NONE of the transparent-corner checks. It must wrap on all four edges and carry no landmark, no light direction and no vignette; per-asset tileWorld overrides the profile.

illustration.note: Venue cards. Bottom fifth stays simple for the name scrim.

portrait.note: Bust crop, centered for circular use, face within central 70%.

ui-icon.note: Test over both the navy shell and bright water.

element.note: Source element for compose.py. NEVER ships on its own — a single penguin is 4-7px at race scale. Lives in art/elements/, not assets/images/.

roles.hazard: Collides or penalizes. Must telegraph before contact and hold the 3:1 contrast floor on Pearl Lagoon AND Glacier Sound.
roles.ambient: Decorative, no collision. MUST NOT be confusable with a hazard at race scale — different silhouette family, not just different color.
roles.landmark: Venue identity, on land or fixed. Never affects play.
roles.traffic: Non-racing boats. MUST NOT be confusable with a competitor at race scale (extends race-view.md 10.2).
roles.nav: Navigation aids the player is meant to read — channel markers, beacons. Canonical buoyage color coding.

anchors.center: Rotation and placement origin at the art's centroid. Floating things.
anchors.waterline: Origin where the object meets the water. Things that stick up out of it.
anchors.trunk-base: Origin at the base of the stem. Trees, reeds.
anchors.footprint: Origin at the center of the ground contact polygon. Buildings, standing birds.

This is the BACK of the animal, never the belly: the body is true black — black is one of this venue's two declared accents, so do not shift it toward navy, steel blue or charcoal — built from flat hard-edged facets, with absolutely no rim light, no outer glow or halo, and no glossy specular highlights. assets.subject: SEVEN EMPEROR penguins crowded together on ice, seen from directly overhead. COMPOSITION IS THE HARD PART — read this first: the group must look like real animals standing around at random, photographed from a drone. Arrange them IRREGULARLY and ASYMMETRICALLY. Absolutely NOT in a circle, ring, radial pattern, rosette, mandala or snowflake, and NOT evenly spaced. The centre of the group must be its DENSEST part, never an empty hole. Some birds should stand closer together than others, a couple should slightly overlap or touch, one or two should sit a little apart from the main mass, and the whole cluster should be lopsided rather than balanced. Headings should be scattered and unrelated to each bird's position — not all turned inward, not all turned outward. Keep the group compact so it fills a roughly circular-but-lumpy footprint. EACH BIRD: a compact teardrop seen from above — a glossy black back and head filling most of the shape, a short beak pointing outward, two dark flippers held slightly away from the body, a sliver of white breast at the front edge, and a vivid orange-yellow ear-and-neck flash. Seven warm yellow flecks scattered through a dark irregular mass is what identifies this species at distance, so keep every flash legible and larger than life. Keep visible dark gaps between most neighbours so the group reads as several distinct animals. Each bird is only about 12 pixels at final size, so give each a clean silhouette, its yellow flash, and nothing else. No ice, no ground, no shadow
assets.note: COMPOSED by compose.py from arctic-penguin-emperor. Two generated huddles came back as rosettes; a PRNG does irregular scatter that a diffusion model will not. Upsized ~50% over strict scale: measured, birds do not resolve below ~70px for a seven-bird group.

assets.subject: a Weddell seal hauled out and resting, seen from directly overhead — a plump elongated torpedo body tapering to paired rear flippers, a small distinctly rounded head set off from the shoulders, and two short fore-flippers held out from the sides. Mottled silver-grey and charcoal in flat hard-edged facets, with a paler belly tone showing along the flanks. CRITICAL: it must read unmistakably as a living animal and never as a rock or a chunk of ice — the head, the neck taper and the fore-flippers are what separate it from a boulder, so keep all three clearly articulated and never let the outline collapse into a plain oval. Naturalistically proportioned, never a cartoon-eyed mascot. No ice, no ground, no shadow

assets.subject: FOUR ADELIE penguins walking in single file on ice, seen from directly overhead. DIRECTION IS CRITICAL: the line of travel runs VERTICALLY up the frame — the last bird near the bottom edge, the leader near the top edge, the others evenly between them on a gently curving track that never departs far from vertical. Every bird faces ALONG the line, i.e. toward the TOP of the frame. Do NOT run the line diagonally or across the frame; the engine rotates this sprite and treats straight up as the direction of travel. VIEWPOINT: from directly above you see the back of each bird's head and its back — no eyes, no face, no chest, with the beak foreshortened and pointing away up the frame. EACH BIRD: a compact teardrop — glossy black back and head filling most of the shape, dark flippers held slightly away from the body, a sliver of white breast at the leading edge only. SPECIES SIGNATURE: Adelies are the PLAIN penguin — solid black head with no yellow anywhere, just a fine white eye ring and a small dull pinkish beak. The absence of warm colour is the identifier; do not add any. Keep spacing close to even but not mechanical, with one bird lagging slightly, and keep every bird clearly separated. Each bird is only about 12 pixels at final size. No ice, no ground, no shadow

assets.subject: a temperate tidal estuary at low water, aerial-oblique, horizon just below the top quarter. THE SAND IS THE DOMINANT COLOR: broad exposed sandbars filling roughly half the picture in confident warm amber-gold, built from bold chunky faceted planes, dry crowns bright and sunlit, wet margins a much darker ochre where the tide has just left, crisp scalloped edges, bold branching drain-runnels cut into them. ONE sinuous channel of DEEP SATURATED SLATE-BLUE water — a rich blue-grey with real blue in it, never neutral grey — winds from the plain empty foreground back toward a distant sea, and it is the eye-path: big angular ripple planes in two clear tones, carrying bright white current streaks and eddy curls that show which way the water is running. A line of leaning rust-red withy markers, bundled sticks, steps irregularly along the channel edge into the distance. The focal element is a small loose group of FOUR SPOON-BILLED SANDPIPERS on the nearest bar — plump little shorebirds with the distinctive flat spatulate spoon-shaped bill tip, warm brown backs and white bellies, bold simplified two-tone shapes rather than feather-by-feather naturalism, one with wings raised, the others feeding head-down. SKY WITH REAL VARIETY: several big rounded blob-stack cumulus of clearly DIFFERENT sizes, each with a single flat shade tone underneath, at different heights, mixed with a few thin horizontal streak clouds — not a uniform band of identical wisps. Green is limited to one thin dark shore line at the horizon and nowhere else. STRICTLY EXCLUDE: neutral grey or desaturated water; muted, washed-out or pastel color; naturalistic wildlife-illustration rendering; long down-curved curlew bills; turquoise or tropical water; flamingos or any pink bird; otters or any mammal; broad green marsh grass; evenly repeated identical clouds; any grass, bird or object in the lower fifth of the frame
assets.note: Regen 4. Pass 1 drifted tropical (marsh/flamingos/otter). Pass 2 specced pewter-pastel, measured 0.185 sat vs set 0.66-0.94 and read unfinished. Pass 3 gold-dominant fixed that but water stayed neutral grey (0.507). Pass 4 cut to 4 large birds; with blue water it reaches 0.693 = in range. This pass: deeper slate blue, varied cumulus, and the spoon-billed sandpipers PINNED BY NAME so they survive regeneration (Wes liked them; the spatulate bill is the charm).

assets.subject: ONE wandering albatross in flight, soaring, seen from directly overhead — enormous slender wings held straight out and locked, not flapping, spanning nearly the full width of the frame and giving the bird a long thin CROSS silhouette unlike anything else. Body and back are white, the upperwing surfaces darken toward the trailing edge and finish in clean black wingtips, and the short wedge tail trails behind. The heavy pale hooked bill leads, pointing to the TOP of the frame. Wings are narrow and stiff with a subtle backward sweep, never broad or rounded. Crisp flat faceted shading, a clean dark contour no heavier than the rest of the set, no glossy speculars, no motion blur. Exactly one bird, alone. No water, no ground, NO SHADOW — the engine draws the shadow that makes it read as airborne

assets.subject: ONE snow petrel in flight, seen from directly overhead, centred and filling the frame, flying toward the TOP. Wings spread and slightly swept back in a shallow M, short wedge tail behind, small head leading. The snow petrel is UNIFORMLY WHITE — body, back, and both wings from shoulder to wingtip, with no dark wingtips, no dark trailing edge and no grey banding. Think of a white dove rather than a gull or an albatross. The only non-white parts are a small black bill and a black eye. Shade the white with the faintest cool grey planes only, just enough to show the wing surfaces turning, and give it a clean thin dark contour so the shape still separates when it passes over pale ice. Crisp flat faceted shading, no glossy speculars, no motion blur. Exactly one bird, alone. No water, no ground, NO SHADOW

assets.subject: ONE polar research hut, alone, seen from DIRECTLY OVERHEAD — a prefab field-station module standing on short skids, so nearly all of what shows is its ROOF. A plain rectangular footprint about half again as long as it is wide, with a shallow gabled roof and one crisp RIDGE LINE running the full length of the long axis, straight up the frame. The ridge splits the roof into two flat planes of clearly different lightness — that hard two-tone split is what makes it read as a solid volume instead of a flat rectangle, so it must be unmistakable. CRITICAL: image models want to draw a building in three-quarter view. There must be NO visible wall face, NO end elevation, NO perspective and NO vanishing point — the roof is a flat rectangle seen square-on, exactly as a building looks in a satellite photograph. COLOUR: painted high-visibility international orange-red, warm and saturated across the whole roof — the deliberate safety colour field huts are painted so they can be found in a whiteout, and the one thing that separates a hut from the rock and ice it sits on. Detail is limited to what survives at 50px: a dark doorway with a small entry step at one gable end, one short dark stove pipe offset to one side of the ridge, and a narrow darker trim band along each eave. Corners are square and crisp and the outline is a clean hard-edged rectangle, never a soft or rounded blob. A thin clean dark contour, no heavier than the rest of the set. No snow, no drift, no ground, no ice, no rock, no cast shadow, no antenna mast, no guy wires, no flag, no people, no vehicles
assets.note: ELEMENT for arctic-station. elementFill 0.64 rather than the profile's 0.88: compose.py rotates with expand=False, so an oblong only survives rotation if it fits inside its own inscribed circle. At 3:2 and 0.88 fill the half-diagonal is 0.53 of the frame and the corners are clipped past ~15deg — unmissable on a building. At 0.64 it is 0.385 and the hut rotates freely at any angle. The group's `scale` range is raised to compensate.

assets.subject: COMPOSED from arctic-hut — see that element for the art.
assets.note: COMPOSED by compose.py — three huts of one design, not three generations. Glacier Sound's first landmark, the arctic counterpart to bayou-shack. TUNED against a 3:2 stand-in rectangle, not guessed: the first numbers (spread 0.46 / minGap 0.80) failed to place all three huts on half of the seeds tried, because scatter() is rejection sampling biased INWARD (r = R*u^0.62) — an arrangement existing geometrically is not the same as the sampler finding it. spread 0.62 / minGap 0.72 fits 3/3 on 40/40 seeds. fillTo 0.86 because frame fill still swings 0.73-1.09 across seeds, which would make `world` mean a different on-screen size per seed; normalizing makes world 170 honest and leaves the seed controlling layout only. 0.86 rather than 0.88 clears the profile's 6% safeMargin tripwire instead of landing exactly on it. Seed 7 chosen by eye from six candidates: three separate buildings in an irregular triangle, where 4 and 31 clump a pair together and 19 and 23 leave a hollow centre. SIZING (measured after ingest, not predicted): fillTo rescales the composition by 0.86/0.65 = 1.32x, so huts land 49-69px on the long axis = 5.3-7.5m at 9.2px/m. That is Jamesway/Weatherhaven module size and deliberately LARGER than the 56px boat — a hut you can live in outsizes a 20ft sportboat. An earlier estimate here said 3.7-6.5m; it omitted the fillTo upscale. `rotate` is deliberately narrow (+/-40deg): station modules sit broadly aligned into the wind, fully random angles read as debris rather than a camp, and zero rotation reads as a copy-paste stamp.

assets.subject: Wind-packed snow lying over sea ice, seen from straight overhead in flat overcast light — a quiet near-white field worked over by wind. Across it run short broken sastrugi: shallow ridges of hard scoured snow, each only a fraction of the frame long, lying in loosely the same direction but at slightly varying angles, never lining up with the edges of the picture. Their crests take the palest white and the scoured troughs settle to a cool blue-grey. Between them sit low drift lobes with soft feathered lips, a scatter of shallow wind-scallops, and a few faint healed cracks reading as thin blue-grey hairlines that fade out rather than running across the frame. Everything is drawn in clean faceted planes with crisp edges — no airbrushed gradients, no fine speckle, no photographic snow grain. The whole image stays inside a tight range from near-white to pale blue-grey. No dark shadow, no exposed blue glacier ice, no rock, no meltwater, no crevasse, no footprints or animal tracks
assets.note: First texture-class asset. tileWorld 512 is measured against this venue, not guessed: the camera is 1:1 and the viewport runs ~1280x800 world units, so a 512 tile repeats ~2.5 x 1.6 per screen — small enough that Glacier Sound's 3000-5000 unit ice masses stop being one flat fill, large enough that the repeat is not countable at a glance. The 1024 master is a 2x supersample of that, so the 4px legibility floor lands at 8px in the master. WIRED: drawIslands() fills fixed `ice`-style land with it as a world-anchored canvas pattern (getSnowPattern in script.js), so it stays nailed to the ice as the camera moves. It ships at SNOW_TEXTURE_ALPHA 0.3 over the flat ISLAND_STYLES.ice body — at full strength it read as a chopped, busy surface that competed with the floes, and 0.5 was still louder than wanted. The blend is baked into the pattern source, so it still costs one fill; measured on screen, land contrast is 0.30x the master's (std 3.1 vs 10.2, range 228-243 vs 189-255). Floes and bergs deliberately keep their baked faceted sprite — they spin, and a world-anchored pattern would slide across a turning floe. Arctic is the only venue authoring `ice` shapes, so nothing else changed. Cost measured against the flat fill it replaced: 0.36 ms/frame in a real racing frame, 1.75 ms/frame with the camera buried in the biggest ice mass.

assets.subject: Bare wind-scoured granite seen from straight overhead in flat overcast light — cold blue-grey rock, hard and dry. It is broken into angular blocks by a network of joints and fractures: straight-edged cracks meeting at blunt angles, dividing the surface into irregular flat plates of slightly different tone, the way frost-shattered rock splits along its grain. A few of the plates are tilted enough to catch a shade lighter or darker than their neighbours, so the rock reads as broken relief rather than a painted slab. Scattered through it are patches of coarser rubble and a scatter of loose angular chips caught in the wider cracks, plus a faint mottling of paler feldspar and darker mineral grain in the stone itself — a suggestion of granite's speckle, drawn as shaped marks, never as fine noise or photographic grit. The whole image holds a narrow range of cold greys around a mid-dark value, with no black voids and no bright highlights. No snow, no frost, no ice, no meltwater, no lichen, no moss, no vegetation, no sand, no soil, no warm brown or orange rock
assets.note: Second texture-class asset, and the one that fixed the class's venue clause: textures used to COMMIT to the venue's dominant hue, which was right for arctic-snow only by coincidence and would have asked for blue rock here. NO SNOW ON IT, deliberately — arctic granite realistically drifts over, but the two textures then converge and rock stops being distinguishable from ice at a glance. `granite` is hard (grounds you) and `ice` is soft (costs speed), so they are different things to the player and must stay different to the eye. tileWorld 256 rather than snow's 512: the three granite shapes are r 90-382, so a 512 tile would show barely one repeat on the largest, and the smaller tile buys 4x supersample from the 1024 master for joint cracks that a 2x would smear. Repetition is a non-issue at these sizes. WIRED at alpha 0.3 through LAND_TEXTURES in script.js (the snow-specific getSnowPattern generalized to getLandPattern(ctx, style, base), keyed style -> {src, tile, alpha}). Until this landed the shapes were FLAT SLABS: bakeIslandSprite's granite facet fan is dead code for authored venues, because compileVenueDoc marks every fixed shape fromMask and that path only fills and strokes. ⚠️ THE BLEND LIGHTENS THE ROCK — the master's mean luma is 124 against the flat body's 84, so 0.3 lands the rock at 94.6 (measured), a 13% lift. Snow had no such shift because its master mean (239) already matched the ice body. If the rock should hold its value, the fix is to normalize the tile's mean to the base before compositing, not to drop the alpha. All three sit within ~400 units of the round-1 mark, so they are passed close aboard every lap.

assets.subject: An inflatable racing mark floating on open water, seen from DIRECTLY OVERHEAD — looking straight down onto it from a helicopter, with none of its side or bottom rim visible anywhere, not even at the near edge. THINK OF IT AS A LOW THREE-SIDED PYRAMID, not a flat cushion. It is a squat tetrahedron: a rounded triangular base with three big triangular faces that SLOPE UPWARD and inward to meet at a single blunt apex directly above the centre. Seen from above you are looking down at those three sloping faces, and the three ridges where they meet run from the central apex out to the three rounded corners, forming a clean three-spoke Y. A bold dark lifting ring sits on the apex at the centre — make it a solid, chunky ring, not a hairline, because it is the one focal dot. THREE FACES, THREE CLEARLY DIFFERENT VALUES — this is the hardest requirement and the whole point of the pyramid form. Because each face tilts in a different direction, each catches the single light source differently. Render them as roughly 100%, 75% and 50% brightness: one face bright, one clearly mid, one clearly dark, with a hard crisp edge along every ridge. The engine desaturates inactive marks to flat slate grey for most of the race, so hue differences are worthless — CONVERTED TO GREYSCALE the three faces, the Y-ridge and the centre ring must all still read instantly. A mark that is one even tone with faint seams is a failure. COLOUR: true safety orange, warm and mid-bright, not red and not scarlet. Flat poster-like colour within each face — absolutely no gloss, no shine, no specular highlight, no smooth gradient, no plastic sheen. A narrow band of deeper wetter orange runs around the very bottom edge where the fabric meets the water. ROTATION: placed at an arbitrary angle with no 'up' — the three faces, ridges and corners must be identical in size and shape so the three-fold symmetry looks deliberate however it is turned, and the apex must sit at the exact centre of the frame. Drawn at only about 30 pixels: bold simple silhouette, a thin clean contour no heavier than the rest of the set, no detail that would not survive that size. No numbers, no letters, no flag, no water, no ripple, no shadow
assets.note: Venue-agnostic: the only prop on all ten venues, so no venue palette clause. Replaces the 160x140 oblique mark.png with a 2048 square master. ENGINE FACTS: drawMarkBodies() draws it at W=30 and applies an arbitrary per-mark rotation, so the art has no 'up' and three-fold symmetry is correct here — the opposite of the group-prop rule against symmetry (hence allowSymmetry). THE INACTIVE-STATE TEST WAS UNWINNABLE AND TWO CANDIDATES WERE REJECTED FOR FAILING IT. getMarkImgGray() tints inactive marks with source-atop rgba(148,163,184,0.8), i.e. 0.2*art + 0.8*slate, so exactly 20% of any value difference survives BY CONSTRUCTION. Measured three-face value spread, active -> inactive: incumbent 54.4 -> 10.9, candidate A 39.7 -> 7.9, this one 28.8 -> 5.8. At 30px all three are the same grey triangle when inactive. Inactive legibility is a CODE parameter, not an art problem: dropping the tint from 0.8 to ~0.55 recovers 45% instead of 20% and visibly helps whatever art is used. SHIPPED: the higher-contrast candidate, chosen by eye. It also measured best of the two new ones on three-face value spread (39.7 active / 7.9 inactive, against the alternative's 28.8 / 5.8), so the preference matched the metric. Its known deviation is colour: body RGB (202,57,9) reads scarlet rather than the safety orange the subject asked for — the incumbent sat at (225,108,44). Left as-is because the extra saturation is part of why it reads at 30px, but if the mark ever looks too red against the warm venues (redrock, swamp), that is the number to change. Sized at world 30 with fillTo 0.96, giving ~29px visible. It went 30 -> 60 while ingest was mis-measuring the master (invisible alpha-1 residue inflated the bbox, so world 60 was only drawing 41px). Once that was fixed the same 60 drew 58px, which was too big, so it came back to 30. The collider markRadius = 12 (24 units across) is unchanged throughout. MARK TAXONOMY (design decision, 2026-07-28): the orange tetrahedron is a TEMPORARY mark — an inflatable laid by the race committee for this race. The yellow can is a PERMANENT mark — a fixed installation the course is built around. Which one a course uses is a per-course choice, not a global one. Currently every course uses the orange temporary mark.

assets.subject: A RED lighted channel buoy floating on open water, seen from DIRECTLY OVERHEAD. COLOUR: the buoy's red is sampled from the venue card and must be matched — a deep warm signal red around #BB3220, never scarlet, never orange, never pink, never maroon. It is a navigation aid, so the red is functional information and must not be shifted toward the surrounding water's hue. MATCH THE BUOYS IN THE LIGHTHOUSE COVE VENUE CARD — the same class of lighted pillar buoy, rendered top-down. Its construction, from the water inward, is a set of CONCENTRIC RINGS: (1) a broad low DRUM FLOAT filling most of the sprite, in the buoy's colour, with a slightly deeper, wetter tone in a narrow band right at its outer waterline edge; (2) a crisp WHITE HORIZONTAL BAND ringing the drum just inside that edge — this bright ring is the buoy's signature and the thing that makes it findable, so keep it clean, unbroken and a full clear step brighter than everything around it; (3) a TAPERED TOWER rising from the centre of the drum, in the same colour, reading from above as a smaller concentric circle a clear step brighter than the drum because it is nearer the light; (4) at the exact centre, the LANTERN: a small pale housing ringed around a DARK POINTED CAP, with a tiny bright finial dot at the very top. The dark cap is the one focal point of the whole sprite. Seen from directly overhead, none of the buoy's side is visible — only these rings, each a flat hard-edged band of clearly different lightness. Those value steps ARE the structure: a concentric object has no silhouette to read by, so the rings must still make complete sense converted to greyscale. Fill the frame — reach close to the edges with only a hair of margin. Engine rotation transforms the coordinate system rather than sampling a fixed frame, so nothing clips at any angle and padding only makes the buoy smaller than it should be. Absolutely no gloss, no shine, no specular highlight, no smooth gradient, no plastic sheen, no reflection. A thin clean dark contour. No numbers, no letters, no text, no flag, no water, no ripple, no shadow

assets.subject: A yellow cylindrical racing mark — the classic inflatable 'yellow can' — floating on open water, seen from DIRECTLY OVERHEAD, with none of its side visible anywhere. From this angle it is a FLAT CIRCULAR DISC with a taut inflated top: a narrow band of deeper, wetter yellow around the waterline, then a broad flat top face, and a bold dark lifting ring sitting at the exact centre as the one focal dot. Three or four faint radial seams run from the ring out to the rim, spaced evenly, reading as slightly darker lines that show the fabric panels. COLOUR: vivid safety yellow, warm and high-visibility, never mustard, never lime, never cream. It must be findable at a glance against pale turquoise shallows, olive swamp water and near-black polar water alike. Fill the frame: the buoy should reach close to the edges, with only a hair of margin. assets.note: Alternative race mark to the orange tetrahedron. Circular and radially symmetric, so it reads identically at any of the arbitrary rotations drawMarkBodies applies. Currently every course uses the orange temporary mark. SHIPPED AND READY BUT UNUSED: drawMarkBodies() resolves a single global markImg, so nothing renders this yet — using it needs marks to carry a sprite reference rather than share one. Measured contrast against water is ~2.4x the orange mark's at every venue (Glacier Sound 10.4:1 vs 4.4, Pearl Lagoon 2.7:1 vs 1.1, Gatorgrass 5.5:1 vs 2.3), and being a circle it is rotation-invariant where the tetrahedron is not.

assets.subject: A race committee boat anchored at the end of a start line, seen from DIRECTLY OVERHEAD, floating level, bow pointing to the TOP of the frame. It is a beamy 30-foot club launch — a working motorboat, never a yacht and never a racing hull: a long hull with a full wide midsection, near-parallel sides through the middle, a bluntly rounded bow, and a SQUARE cut-off transom across the stern. ABSOLUTELY NO SAIL, NO MAST, NO BOOM, NO RIGGING, no sail number, and nothing triangular anywhere on the deck — seen from directly above a racing sailboat is a pair of white triangles, and the single worst failure this sprite can have is being mistaken for one of the boats racing around it. THE READ IS A DARK CORE INSIDE A WHITE OUTLINE, which is the exact inverse of a sailboat's white sails inside a dark hull line — this is the whole point of the design. Working from the bow aft: a short pale foredeck with a small dark windlass block at its tip; then a hard-edged RECTANGULAR DECKHOUSE filling the forward half of the boat, its flat roof CHARCOAL and the darkest thing in the sprite, carrying one small pale dome at its centre; then a clear step of pale open deck; then a MID-NAVY canvas awning stretched over the open aft cockpit as a second rectangle, clearly LIGHTER than the charcoal roof so the two never merge into one smear. The white of the hull survives only as a clean margin running all the way around that dark core, widening at the bow and across the transom. THE SIGNATURE IS AN ORANGE FLAG, and it must be unmistakable. A short staff stands on the after deck and a bold rectangular safety-orange flag streams STRAIGHT AFT from it, out past the transom and clear of the hull, breaking the silhouette at the stern — the boat lies head to wind, so the flag blows down the frame. Render it as one flat solid orange rectangle with a slight ripple in its trailing edge, big enough to be the second thing the eye finds after the hull. This flag is what tells the player where the starting line ends, so it is functional information: keep it true safety orange and never shift it toward the colour of the water. COLOUR AND VALUE: clean off-white hull and deck with a single crisp deep-navy stripe following the sheerline the whole way around, charcoal deckhouse roof, mid-navy awning, safety-orange flag. Those extremes are deliberate — this sprite has to be findable on near-black polar water, where the white hull and the flag carry it, AND on pale turquoise shallows, where the charcoal roof and the navy stripe carry it. CONVERTED TO GREYSCALE the hull margin, the two roof rectangles and the flag must still read as separate steps. Flat hard-edged shading in clear steps of lightness, absolutely no gloss, no shine, no specular highlight, no smooth gradient, no plastic sheen, no reflection. A thin clean dark contour, no heavier than the rest of the set. Drawn at only about 85 pixels: bold simple shapes and no detail that would not survive that size. No crew, no figures, no water, no wake, no spray, no ripple, no anchor line, no cast shadow, no numbers, no letters, no lettering on the hull
assets.note: SHIPPED. A third mark KIND for the line ends, alongside the orange inflatable (temporary) and the yellow can (permanent): the vessel the line is sighted from. venuedoc's MARK_KINDS is now the one list — validator, editor dropdown and script.js's sprite registry all read it — and the eval fixtures already named the ends `sf-pin` and `sf-boat`, so the concept predated the art. VENUE-NEUTRAL like mark/zodiac/buoy-channel-*: race furniture at all ten venues, no palette clause. ROLE IS `traffic`, NOT `nav`, even though it is functionally a mark — the nav add-on emits 'use canonical buoyage shape and colour coding', which is buoy language and would push a boat toward red/green. The contract that binds is traffic's: never confusable with a competitor. The mark-function requirements (the orange flag, the line end) live in the subject text instead. SIZING: world 92 with fillTo 0.92 gives 37x85px = 9.2m at 9.2px/m, a 30ft club launch and 1.5x the 56px racing boat. That gap is the OPPOSITE call from the zodiac, which is deliberately SHORTER than a racer: a support RIB stays off the competitor read by being small, a committee boat by being big, boxy and white. 85px on an 1100-unit start line is 7.7% of it. Content filled 0.757 of the master, so fillTo upscales 1.22x — visible softening at 1024, invisible at 85. MEASURED CONTRAST (WCAG vs median water, at true race scale): Glacier Sound median 1.28:1 but brightest 10% 9.74:1; Pearl Lagoon median 2.84:1 with darkest 10% 5.32:1. That split IS the design — the white hull carries it on near-black water, the charcoal roof on pale turquoise — and both ends beat the zodiac (2.53 / 2.27 median). Judge it on the plates, as the zodiac's note argues: the player's own hull is 2.01:1 on lagoon. THREE RECORDED DEVIATIONS, none blocking. (1) The orange flag does NOT break the silhouette as the subject demanded: it is 107px of a 337px beam, entirely inside the hull footprint, and streams to starboard rather than aft. At 85px it is a ~12px orange dash on the white transom and still reads on both plates, but it is less findable than the macaroni-crest trick intended. If the line end is ever hard to spot, that is what to redraw. (2) A ~14px transparent slot separates a detached 13px navy contour ring from the hull, a background-remover artifact; 1.5px at race scale and invisible on the plates. (3) Teak deck striping is microtexture beyond spec and blurs to tan. Ingest passed with no warnings. ENGINE, ALL THREE BLOCKERS NOW FIXED. (1) drawMarkBodies resolved a single global markImg; it now resolves MARK_SPRITES[kind], which also lights up mark-can-yellow after a week shipped-but-unused. (2) It rotated every mark by an arbitrary per-position scramble, right for a tetrahedron and wrong for a vessel. orientCourseMarks() now freezes a heading from the LINE'S OWN NORMAL, signed by the direction of travel on the line's FIRST route use — not from the live wind (which oscillates every frame, so the hull would swing with every puff and the baked flag would fight the real breeze) and not per leg (a line sailed twice would spin the boat 180 degrees when the fleet came back to finish). The wobble stays: on a hull it reads as lying to an anchor. (3) markRadius 12 is now a per-mark body — a 3-circle r=19 capsule for the hull, and the sprite is nudged 19 units outboard along the line so the line's sailable span stays clear with the flagstaff on the mark point. Every consumer is written as (constant + bodyR) so a buoy's bodyR of 12 reproduces the old 50 and 115 exactly. Covered by eval/test_marks.js. The committee boat belongs on the STARBOARD end of its line; venuedoc warns when it is not, rather than enforcing it, because it is a convention. NOT YET PLACED ON ANY VENUE — that is an authoring decision, and it must not land on Sea Trial Bay, which is the eval anchor.

assets.subject: A rigid-hull inflatable boat — a Zodiac-type work RIB — seen from DIRECTLY OVERHEAD, floating level, bow pointing to the TOP of the frame. THE SILHOUETTE IS THE WHOLE POINT: two fat parallel buoyancy tubes run the length of the boat and sweep together into a blunt rounded point at the bow, leaving a long open U-shaped well between them, and the stern is cut square and OPEN across the back — a horseshoe, never a pointed racing hull. The tubes read as thick cylinders, tapering to sealed conical ends at the transom, banded by three or four dark seams. Inside the well: a flat pale deck, one small dark centre console set just forward of amidships, and a plain bench seat behind it. A dark blocky outboard motor sits on the transom and overhangs the stern beyond the tubes. ABSOLUTELY NO SAIL, NO MAST, NO BOOM, NO RIGGING and no sail number — this is a powered working boat and must never be mistaken for a racing sailboat at a glance. COLOUR: bright safety orange tubes, warm and saturated, the canonical colour of a rescue and support RIB, with a mid-grey deck and near-black console and outboard for internal contrast. It has to stay findable against near-black polar water, deep blue and pale turquoise shallows alike. Flat hard-edged shading in clear steps of lightness, no gloss, no specular highlight, no smooth gradient. A thin clean dark contour, no heavier than the rest of the set. No water, no wake, no spray, no ripple, no cast shadow, no crew, no figures, no flag
assets.note: VENUE-NEUTRAL like mark/buoy-channel-*: a support RIB is race furniture at every venue — committee boat, safety boat, and Glacier Sound's station tender for arctic-station. Kept venue-neutral deliberately so no palette clause tints it; safety orange is canonical everywhere. SIZING: world 54 with fillTo 0.92 gives a 50px hull = 5.4m at 9.2px/m, a real Zodiac Pro size and deliberately SHORTER than the 56px racing boat. That size gap is part of the `traffic` contract, but the silhouette does the real work: a horseshoe of tubes with an open transom shares no family with a pointed sailing hull, and it survives colour removal. Do NOT exaggerate it up to boat size for readability — that trades away the one thing keeping it off the competitor read. MEASURED CONTRAST (WCAG ratio vs flat water, at 54px): Glacier Sound — orange tubes 4.22:1, median pixel 2.53:1. Pearl Lagoon — median 2.27:1, tubes only 1.36:1, because orange and turquoise are opposed in HUE but nearly equal in LUMINANCE, so on lagoon water this prop is carried by hue and by its dark contour, not by value. That reads as a fail against the 3:1 floor until you measure the thing the floor is calibrated on: the player's own hull is 2.01:1 on Pearl Lagoon, WORSE than this. BODY COVERING: this creature is covered in smooth wet skin with fine scales, and nothing else — no feathers and no plumage, no fur, no wings. PFD COLOURS, and these are exact: the main body of the jacket is bright vivid red (#E10600); the foam panels across the chest and the shoulder straps are bright amber-gold (#FFD84D); the waist webbing is charcoal with a plain metal buckle. assets.subject: A small coastal container ship underway, seen from DIRECTLY OVERHEAD, floating level, bow pointing to the TOP of the frame. TRUE PLAN VIEW AT BOTH ENDS, and the SILHOUETTE IS A LONG ROUNDED-TOP RECTANGLE: a flat straight bottom edge — the transom, spanning the full beam, the last thing in the image — two long parallel sides, and only the top fifth tapering to a small bluntly rounded nose, never a needle or dagger point. The hull does NOT round off at the bottom: it stops dead on that straight transom line, with nothing drawn below it — no darker band, no bevel, no step, no rounded stern face. Every generation so far has rounded or stepped the stern, and every one was wrong. It is a working cargo vessel — never a yacht, never a warship, never a ferry and never a racing hull: one long slab-sided hull with near-parallel sides through most of its length. ABSOLUTELY NO SAIL, NO MAST, NO BOOM, NO RIGGING, no sail number and no white triangle anywhere on deck — seen from directly above a racing sailboat is a pair of white triangles, and this ship shares the water with ten of them. THE READ, FROM BOW AFT: a short triangular FORECASTLE deck at the stem, drawn in the hull's own colour and carrying one small dark anchor-windlass block; then the CARGO FIELD filling the middle three-fifths of the hull — shipping containers in crisp transverse BAYS with a thin seam of bare deck between one bay and the next, so the whole field reads as a rhythm of coloured bands separated by dark deck lines, the banded top-down signature of a real container ship; then, hard aft, a crisp WHITE SUPERSTRUCTURE BLOCK spanning the full beam — the bridge — the brightest thing in the sprite, and just behind the bridge the funnel — which from directly above is nothing but a SMALL DARK FLAT CIRCLE on the deck, because a chimney seen from its top is only its rim: never a cone, never a cylinder with visible sides, never anything with height. THE HULL IS GRAPHITE CHARCOAL, surviving as a clean dark margin running all the way around the cargo field, widening at the bow and across the transom. CONTAINER SIZE IS THE SCALE CUE, and it is the clause to get right: each bay is a band of SIX NARROW containers side by side spanning nearly the full beam — each container an UPRIGHT rectangle roughly three times taller than it is wide, its long side running fore-and-aft. Many small slabs are what make this read as an enormous vessel; a bay of two or three oversized boxes makes it read as a toy tug, which is the single worst failure this sprite can have. THE CONTAINERS ARE THE SHIP'S COLOUR, BRIGHT AND CLEAN: vivid saturated jewel tones — crimson, sunflower yellow, emerald green, cobalt blue, crisp white — never black or charcoal, because a dark slab on the deck reads as a hole rather than a container — no two touching containers the same colour, and one or two slots left empty showing dark deck beneath, so the field reads as loaded cargo rather than a printed pattern. EACH CONTAINER IS ONE FLAT SLAB OF ONE FLAT COLOUR: no corrugation, no ribbing, no stripes inside a slab, no lettering, no logos, and no thick black outline drawn around each box — the thin dark deck seams are what separate them. THE VENUE'S SIGNAL COLOURS STAY OFF THE SHIP ITSELF: the hull, deck, forecastle and superstructure never use buoy red, buoy green or safety orange, and NO CONTAINER IS ORANGE — the orange inflatable race marks belong to the player's course reading. VALUE STEPS: converted to greyscale, the dark hull margin, the mid-tone container field and the white bridge block must read as three separate steps — the white bridge sitting at the stern is functional information, telling the player at a glance which end is which and therefore which way the ship is moving. Flat hard-edged shading in clear steps of lightness, no gloss, no shine, no specular highlight, no smooth gradient, no reflection. A thin clean dark contour, no heavier than the rest of the set — never a fat sticker outline. Absolutely no rim light, no outer glow, no halo, no backlight, no vignette and no drawn drop shadow; the background is one flat uniform colour edge to edge. No crew, no figures, no water, no wake, no bow wave, no spray, no cast shadow, no crane, no derrick, no cables, no flags, no text or numbers anywhere

scale.anchor: The player's boat. Hull is ~56 world units (see the repositionBoats comment in script.js) and the camera is 1:1, so 56px = one boat.
scale.boatLength: Treat the boat as a ~20ft (6.1m) sportboat. Nothing in the game names a class, so this is a free choice — and it is the one that makes the accepted art self-consistent. At J/105 scale (10.5m) everything already accepted would be ~2x oversize.
scale.note: Exaggeration is permitted and often required: a penguin's true overhead footprint is ~0.5m = 4.6px, which cannot carry a silhouette. Measured on arctic water, a 7-bird huddle needs ~70px before individual birds resolve and species colour appears. Exaggerate deliberately and record it here; do not drift.

pod.note: calf count decided once per pod; calves take the trailing indices

variance.source: hash(index, channel) — deterministic, never Math.random, so the render path cannot perturb the RNG stream the eval harness depends on

notes: surfaceDepth is deliberately NOT zero — a swimming orca is never fully out of the water, and bottoming the depth curve at 0 draws it flat on the surface like a decal.
The depth curve DWELLS: rise, swim up top, sink, stay down. A sine spends equal time everywhere and reads as bobbing.

Deep animals draw as a flat dark silhouette (#0a1a2c via source-atop), not as the faded real sprite. Losing the markings is what reads as UNDER water; a faded sprite reads as merely far away. Drone footage shows the opposite — markings persist at depth — but legibility at 40px beat accuracy here.

The blow is emitted in WORLD space at the animal's position when it blew, and stays put while the animal swims on. Evaluated analytically from past time, so there is no particle list and nothing to reset between races.
Blow density peaks at exhalation and only falls. Holding peak opacity while the sprite scales up reads as fading IN, which is a bug that took three passes to see.
Rejected after trying: bow wake, submerging foam, fluke prints as rings, and fluke prints as bubble scatters. All read as graphics rather than water.
